summary: GMPLS Ethernet Label Switching extended RSVP-TE to set up Ethernet LSPs, and IEEE CFM provides OAM for checking connectivity. This document defines RSVP-TE extensions to configure CFM OAM on these Ethernet LSPs for fault detection and recovery triggering.

eli5.summary: Once a path is built, you want to check it keeps working. This RFC lets the setup message also switch on the health checks for an Ethernet path.

subtitle: How RSVP-TE signaling can switch on Ethernet connectivity monitoring at the same time as it sets up an Ethernet LSP.

tldr.problem: Ethernet label switched paths set up with GMPLS need connectivity monitoring (IEEE CFM) to detect faults, but configuring the monitoring endpoints separately on every node is laborious.
tldr.mechanism: The RSVP-TE Path message carries an OAM Configuration TLV with a new Ethernet OAM Configuration Sub-TLV holding the MD level, names, MEP IDs, CCM interval and priority, so the end points are configured as the LSP is signaled.
tldr.outcome: It adds new TLVs, error sub-codes and IANA registrations, and supports without modifying the IEEE and ITU-T OAM mechanisms.

today: RFC 7369 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it builds on the generic OAM configuration framework in RFC 7260.

sections.title: Background and Scope
sections.content:
Work on GMPLS Ethernet Label Switching (GELS) extended the GMPLS control plane to establish explicitly routed Ethernet connections (RFC 5828, RFC 6060). The RFC calls these connections Ethernet LSPs. They build on Provider Backbone Bridging - Traffic Engineering (PBB-TE), which lets external control mechanisms create explicitly routed Ethernet connections.

IEEE Connectivity Fault Management (CFM) adds a monitoring flow to check that Ethernet connections are alive, and ITU-T Y.1731 extends CFM with more OAM functions. RFC 7260 defines how RSVP-TE configures OAM in a technology-agnostic way. RFC 7369 adds the Ethernet-specific pieces: it supports, but does not modify, the IEEE and ITU-T mechanisms.
sections.eli5: An Ethernet LSP is a pre-planned route for data. OAM is the set of health checks that tell you if the route still works, and this RFC shows how to switch those checks on while the route is being set up.

sections.title: Ethernet OAM in Brief
sections.content:
The RFC covers proactive connectivity monitoring and assumes on-demand OAM functions are handled by the management plane. A PBB-TE point-to-point Ethernet Switched Path (ESP) is a unidirectional connection identified by three values: destination MAC address, source MAC address and a VLAN identifier (ESP-VID). A bidirectional connection combines two co-routed ESPs. Because the OAM mechanisms are only fully functional on bidirectional connections with co-routed ESPs, the document covers only bidirectional point-to-point PBB-TE connections.

At each end sits a MEP (Maintenance Entity Group End Point). MEPs on one connection share the same Maintenance Domain Level (MD Level) and Maintenance Association Identifier (MAID), and each has its own MEP ID. They exchange Continuity Check Messages (CCMs) at a fixed interval. If three consecutive CCMs are lost, connectivity failure is declared, and the detecting MEP sets the Remote Defect Indicator (RDI) bit in the CCMs it sends. A MEP that receives a CCM with RDI set immediately declares failure. Optional MIPs (intermediate points) at transit nodes help localize failures.
sections.eli5: The two ends of the path keep sending each other "still here?" pings. If three in a row go missing, they decide the path is broken and tell the other end.

sections.title: How Signaling Sets Up the OAM
sections.content:
The LSP Attribute Flags "OAM MEP entities desired" and "OAM MIP entities desired" from RFC 7260 signal that OAM entities must be established. An OAM Configuration TLV goes in the LSP_ATTRIBUTES or LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES object, and the Ethernet-specific data rides in a new Ethernet OAM Configuration Sub-TLV inside it.

The initiator's Path message allocates an upstream label (its MAC address as ESP-MAC A plus a locally chosen VID) and MUST include the OAM Configuration TLV with OAM Type set to Ethernet OAM, the OAM Function Flags Sub-TLV, and an Ethernet OAM Configuration Sub-TLV with the CCM interval and MD level. It MAY add an MD Name Sub-TLV, MUST add a Short MA Name Sub-TLV, and MUST include a MEP ID Sub-TLV with two distinct values for the local and remote MEPs.

The remote node uses the UPSTREAM_LABEL to learn the initiator's reachability, allocates its own label (ESP-MAC B and ESP-VID2), and configures its MEP. When the Resv message reaches the initiator, the initiator reads the remote reachability from the Label object and configures its own MEP. Parameters such as MD level, CCM interval and MEP ID values are chosen outside this document.
sections.eli5: The first message carries a settings card for the health checks. The other end reads it, fills in its own address, and the reply lets the first end finish its own setup.

sections.title: The Ethernet OAM Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The Ethernet OAM Configuration Sub-TLV is type 32 and has a Version field (the CFM protocol version), an MD Level field, reserved bits and a list of nested sub-TLVs. It MUST be carried in the OAM Configuration TLV.

  • MD Name (type 1, optional): a format, a name length and the name. If there is no MD name, the MA name must uniquely identify the Maintenance Association.
  • Short MA Name (type 2, MUST be present): same layout. The combined length of MD Name and Short MA Name MUST be at most 44 bytes.
  • MEP ID (type 3, MUST be present): a Local and a Remote MEP ID, each a 16-bit value in the range 1-8191, each followed by Transmit (T) and Receive (R) flags. When T is set the MEP MUST send OAM packets; when R is set it MUST expect to receive them.
  • Continuity Check (type 4, MUST be present): a priority nibble and a CCM Interval. If the priority's top bit is 0, the CCM priority comes from node defaults; if 1, the next 3 bits set it. The CCM Interval MUST use the 3-bit encoding of IEEE 802.1Q.

Proactive performance monitoring can use the control plane too. Dual-ended Loss Measurement is enabled by setting the Performance Monitoring/Loss and Continuity Check function flags and including the Ethernet OAM Configuration Sub-TLV; no additional configuration is needed.
sections.eli5: The settings card has boxes: a name for the group of checks, an ID number for each end, how often to ping, and how important the pings should be.

sections.title: Errors When a Node Cannot Comply
sections.content:
RFC 7369 defines six new Error Value sub-codes under the "OAM Problem" error code from RFC 7260. A node MUST generate the matching error when it cannot honor the request.

  • Unsupported OAM Version, if the CFM version is not supported.
  • Unsupported MD Level.
  • Unknown MD Name Format and Unknown MA Name Format, for undefined name formats.
  • Name Length Problem, if the MD Name and Short MA Name together exceed 44 bytes.
  • Unsupported CC Interval, if the requested CCM interval is not supported.

This lets the initiator learn exactly which part of the OAM request was refused rather than just that signaling failed.
sections.eli5: If the other end cannot do what the settings card asks, it sends back a note saying which setting was the problem.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The document introduces no additional security issues beyond those in RFC 7260 and RFC 6060. It does add one angle: because OAM entities are created automatically from RSVP-TE messages, a remote attacker could overload a network element by requesting liveliness monitoring of many LSPs with frequent periodic messages. The RFC says message integrity and node authentication prevent this, and points to the RSVP security procedures of RFC 2747 and the security framework in RFC 5920.

IANA allocated OAM Type 1 (Ethernet OAM) and sub-TLV type 32 in the "RSVP-TE OAM Configuration Registry", created an Ethernet Sub-TLVs sub-registry (0-65534 by IETF Review, 65535 experimental), and assigned error values 7 to 12 under "OAM Problem".
sections.eli5: Someone could try to flood a switch with requests to watch too many paths. Checking that messages are genuine keeps that from working.

fields.name: Local MEP ID
fields.desc: MEP ID on the initiator side, 1-8191.

fields.desc: Transmit: the MEP MUST send OAM packets.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Receive: the MEP MUST expect OAM packets.

fields.name: Remote MEP ID
fields.desc: MEP ID for the receiving side, 1-8191.

fields.name: T
fields.desc: Transmit flag for the remote MEP.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Receive flag for the remote MEP.
